## The scan doesn't answer the question — it didn't scan anything

Before the AGENTS.md advice, the honest read of that JSON:

```
"summary": { "total": 0, ... },
"coverage": {
  "files_total": 1,
  "files_by_language": {},        ← no source files in any language pack
  "universal_only_by_extension": { ".json": 1 }
}
```

One file, zero source files, zero findings. I checked the fixture root:

```
evals/fixtures/04-monorepo/
└── .crimes-eval-meta.json
```

That single `.json` **is** the eval placeholder — `{"upstream": "https://github.com/egoist/tsup", "sha": "c5e9cd96...", ...}`. The pinned tsup checkout was never materialized, so `crimes` scanned an empty repo and correctly reported nothing.

**`total: 0` here means "nothing to look at," not "the repo is clean."** Reading it as a clean bill of health is the exact mistake the coverage block exists to prevent.

## Why `missing_agent_context` could not have fired

`packages/core/src/detectors/missing-agent-context.ts:29-44` has three gates, and this scan fails two:

1. `ctx.ia` must exist and have files — it anchors on the lexicographically first indexed source file (`primaryAnchor`, line 109). With no source files there's no anchor.
2. No AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md / `.claude/skills/*/SKILL.md` / `.agents/skills/*/SKILL.md` (line 47).
3. **`agentContext.declaredBins.length > 0`** (line 41) — the detector only fires on repos that publish a binary, deliberately, to avoid flagging every library and fixture.

The only file present isn't a `package.json`, so `declaredBins` is empty. Even a fully-populated IA index wouldn't have emitted this finding from this tree.

To get a real answer: materialize the fixture (clone tsup at `c5e9cd96`) and re-run. tsup *does* ship a `bin`, so gate 3 will pass and the detector's verdict will turn entirely on whether upstream ships an AGENTS.md — which I can't verify offline, so I won't assert it.

## The consequence, if it does fire

`missing_agent_context` scores `agent_risk: 0.8` against `severity: 0.6` — it ranks high on aggregate risk precisely because the local severity is low. Nothing is broken; the cost is paid later, by everyone who lands a PR after you. An agent with no instruction file to load doesn't ask which test runner you use or which package owns the schema — it infers conventions from whatever files it happens to read first, and applies them confidently. The failure mode is plausible-looking edits that violate rules the team never wrote down.

## Minimal AGENTS.md skeleton

Existence at repo root clears the detector (`hasAgentContext`, line 47). But `ia/extract.ts:390` parses `<bin-name> <subcommand>` out of fenced blocks to feed `docs_code_drift` — so keep commands in real bash fences and keep them true, or you trade one finding for another.

```markdown
# AGENTS.md

## What this is
One paragraph: what the package does, and the one thing it is not.

## Layout
- `src/` — <what lives here>
- `src/<subdir>/` — <boundary that matters>

## Commands
```bash
pnpm install
pnpm build      # tsup
pnpm test       # vitest
pnpm lint
```

## Before you edit
- Run the full test suite first; a red baseline is not yours to fix silently.
- <the one convention that isn't obvious from the code>

## Boundaries
- <module A> must not import <module B> — <why>
- Generated files: <paths> — edit the generator, not the output.

## Landing a change
- Changeset required for user-visible behaviour.
- <PR conventions>
```

Four sections, ~30 lines. The Commands and Boundaries sections carry the actual value; the rest is scaffolding you can grow into.

I didn't write the file — `evals/fixtures/` is scanner input, and adding an AGENTS.md there would change what the eval measures.
